newsitem.title: USA: U.S. property insurers post small gain in Q2 net.
newsitem.headline: U.S. property insurers post small gain in Q2 net.

text.p: The U.S. property and casualty insurance industry posted a small gain in consolidated after-tax net income in the 1996 second quarter, reflecting severe price competition in the industry, industry figures showed.

Second quarter after-tax net income was $4.4 billion, up slightly from $4.0 billion in the year-ago period, according to the figures from Insurance Services Office Inc and the National Association of Independent Insurers.
The figures are consolidated estimates for the entire industry based on the reports of insurers that account for 96 percent of the U.S. property-casualty business.

"With the industry facing the potential of large losses in the current lively hurricane season, the lackluster results from the second quarter ... provide no comfort to management," Sean Mooney, senior vice president and economist for the Insurance Information Institute said in a statement.
Meanwhile, the industry continued to show lackluster profitability, with a rate of return of just 7.4 percent on an annualized basis, Mooney said.
That rate of return was about the same as U.S. Treasury bonds, "clearly illustrating the poor profit picture of the industry," Mooney said in a statement.

"An investor can get the same return from investing in U.S. Treasury bonds as in the property-casualty insurance industry and lose no sleep through fears of hurricanes and earthquakes and an unpredictable litigation system," Mooney said.
Net income, which consisted of $4.3 billion in operating income and $1.1 billion in realized capital gains, was helped by a decline in the industry's pre-tax underwriting loss.
Operating income consisted of a pre-tax underwriting loss of $4.4 billion and pre-tax net investment income of $8.9 billion.
The second quarter pre-tax underwriting loss of $4.4 billion compared with a $6.1 billion loss a year ago.
However, net investment income in the second quarter fell 4.2 percent to $8.9 billion from $9.3 billion a year ago.
And realized capital gains fell to $1.1 billion in the 1996 second quarter, down 38.5 percent, from $1.9 billion in 1995.
Mooney said the most notable feature of the second quarter results was the significant decline in investment returns.
Written premiums totaled $66.8 billion for the second quarter of 1996, up 2.6 percent from $65.1 billion in the year-ago period.
The industry showed an improvement in underwriting results, with the underwriting loss declining to $4.4 billion in the second quarter from $6.1 billion in the year-ago period.
But this was partly because catastrophe losses fell to $1.7 billion in the 1996 second quarter from $3.0 billion in the 1995 second quarter.
The uninspiring results reflect severe competition, particularly in commercial lines, Mooney said.
"We are not yet seeing price cutting at a rate that triggered the downturn of the mid-1980s," he said.

"Companies are bleeding from capillaries and small veins, but arteries have not yet been severed. It will take a major shock, and we may get one this hurricane season, to cause a hardening in prices," he said.
-- Patricia Vowinkel 212-859-1716
